title: Debugging Terraform
intro: When Terraform fails with a vague provider error, or applies take forever, these are the tools for seeing what's actually happening underneath.

steps.prompt: An apply fails with a cryptic 'error creating resource: 400'. Re-run it with full debug logging.
steps.fake_output:
[DEBUG] provider.terraform-provider-aws: HTTP Request Sent: POST https://ec2.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/
[DEBUG] provider.terraform-provider-aws: HTTP Response Received: 400 InvalidParameterValue: Value (t3.nano-typo) for parameter instanceType is invalid.
steps.explanation: The debug log shows the raw API request and response — including the actual cloud provider's error message.
steps.why: Terraform's summary error often loses detail the cloud API actually returned. TF_LOG=DEBUG is extremely verbose; add TF_LOG_PATH=./tf.log to write it to a file instead of flooding your terminal — and scrub it before sharing, since it can contain credentials.

steps.prompt: Generate the dependency graph to understand why Terraform creates resources in the order it does.
steps.explanation: Output is in DOT format — an edge from A to B means A depends on B.
steps.why: Terraform infers order from references between resources. When something is created in the wrong order, the graph usually reveals a missing reference — fixed by referencing an attribute, or as a last resort with depends_on.

steps.prompt: An apply is hitting the cloud provider's API rate limits. Re-run it with fewer concurrent operations.
steps.fake_output:
aws_route53_record.a[0]: Creating...
aws_route53_record.a[1]: Creating...
...
Apply complete! Resources: 40 added, 0 changed, 0 destroyed.
steps.explanation: Default parallelism is 10 concurrent operations; lowering it slows things down but stays under rate limits.
steps.why: -parallelism=1 also turns a confusing interleaved log into a sequential one — sometimes the fastest way to pin down which resource actually triggers an error.

steps.prompt: Print the full plan as JSON to feed it into a policy check that blocks any plan destroying a database.
steps.explanation: The JSON plan lists each resource change with its exact actions.
steps.why: This is how policy-as-code tools (OPA/Conftest, Sentinel, Checkov) inspect plans in CI. Here it caught a database about to be destroyed and recreated — the kind of change a human skimming plan output at 6pm might miss.
